newsitem.title: USA: U.S. legislators condemn Europe's stance on Boeing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. legislators condemn Europe's stance on Boeing.

text.p: The United States reacted to the European Union's growing opposition to the Boeing Corp.- McDonnell Douglas Corp. merger on Wednesday, even before its formal rejection in Brussels, Belgium.
The European Commission votes on the $14 billion merger next Wednesday and is likely to block it.

Members of Congress denounced the EU stance as outrageous and ludicrous, and the Senate late on Wednesday unanimously approved a measure condemning the European Union for its expected rejection of the merger.
At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry measured his words.

"We think the principles of competitiveness are those that ought to attend to the European Union's consideration" of the merger, he said. He added the decision should "be done consistently with antitrust law as it's applied within the (European) Union."

McCurry said the government had been in consultation with EU authorities in the last 48 to 72 hours. Top administration officials met at the White House on Tuesday to consider ways to retaliate against the Europeans if they make good their threat to block the merger, the Washington Post reported on Thursday.

While no decisions were made at the meeting, the officials agreed to put the full weight of the government behind Boeing now that the Federal Trade Commission has approved the deal, the newspaper said, quoting administration sources.
Members of Congress were scathing in their criticism of the European stand.

"We could be heading for a major trade war with the EU over this," Representative Norm Dicks, a Washington state Democrat who has Boeing workers in his district, said. "If they make unrealistic demands, the United States government is going to have to retaliate."

Republican Sen. Slade Gorton, also from Boeing's home state of Washington, late on Wednesday introduced and won unanimous approval for an amendment to the $13.2 billion foreign aid appropriation for fiscal 1998, which starts in October.

"The sole true reason for the European Commission's criticism and imminent disapproval of the merger is to gain an unfair competitive advantage for Airbus, a government-owned aircraft manufacturer," Gorton said in a statement.
The amendment directs President Bill Clinton to "take necessary action to protect thousands of U.S. aerospace jobs," Gorton said.
California Republican Representative Ron Packard suggested the EU should approve the deal because the U.S. Federal Trade Comission did.
"They found no cause for concern," he said of the FTC decision. "The EU is simply holding this merger hostage for a sweeter deal."
Representative Jim Talent, a Missouri Republican, said, "The EU can't tell American companies how to do business." He said it was "ludicrous for the EU to turn around and dismiss" the FTC ruling.

Language was equally strong across the Atlantic, where French President Jacques Chirac backed the European Commission's preliminary votes condemning the merger, charging the merger "could be extremely dangerous for Europeans."
Sen. Christopher Bond, a Missouri Republican, replied: "I am surprised that the leader of France would characterise it in such a manner. I believe that he is overreacting."
In Bonn German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the concessions offered by Boeing did not go far enough.
But Boeing announced in Brussels that it would offer no more concessions, arguing it had negotiated in good faith.
A rejection of the deal puts the EU in uncharted waters. One possibility is that Boeing and McDonnell Douglas could make concessions to the Europeans and resubmit their bid.
Or they could take their case to the European Court of Justice, a process that typically takes two years and has never overturned a decision on a major merger.

If Boeing defies the ban and merges anyway, the European Union could fine the combined company up to 10 percent of its annual sales worldwide. Sources say the EU could also seize any new Boeing planes delivered in Europe.

More may be learned soon after the decision. Only hours after the EU makes a formal decision on Wednesday in Brussels, Boeing Chairman Phil Condit and McDonnell Douglas President Harry Stonecipher will testify before the House Subcommittee on Aviation.
FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky and Hugo Paemen, the European Union's ambassador to the United States, may also testify.
